Qui mortem subeundo ex ordinatione Dei sustinuit poenam debitam non peccatis solummodo quarundam singularium personarum, sed universi humani generis: ejus passio virtute ejusdem ordinationis est applicabilis non certis solummodo et definitis personis, sed cuivis humani generis individuo. Sed Christus moriendo sustinuit poenam debitam peccatis totius mundi: Ergo voluit suam mortem esse tanquam universalem causam salutis omnibus applicabilem. Qui Majorem negat, tenetur ostendere cur Deus voluerit Filium suum portare peccata humani generis, si noluerit in ejus morte causam instituere saltem applicabilem humano generi, quamvis applicatio efficax in multis non sequatur. Nos hujus rei alias causas excogitare non possumus, quam quod Divinae bonitati et sapientiae placuerit a redemtore nostro exigere, et quasi in manus suas recipere, lytron universale omnibus applicabile. 1. Ut in ipsa applicatione libertas Divinae voluntatis de suo facientis quod vult, et specialis eudokia erga electos, magis eminere. 2. Ut erga non-electos, saltem in Ecclesia vocatos, misericordiae magnae specimen praeberet. 3. Ut increduli in conscientiis suis revincantur, ex parte Christi non defuisse modum illis liberandis, sed illos sibi defuisse, juxta dictum Christi, Johann. v. 40: Non vultis venire ad me, ut vitam habeatis.

Jam ad Minorem descendamus, in qua affirmatur, Christum sustinuisse poenam debitam peccatis humani generis. Sic loquuntur Scripturae: Omnes nos, ut oves, erravimus: quisque in viam suam nos convertimus: et Jehovah facit ut incurrat in eum poena omnium nostrum, Isa. liii. 6. Sic loquuntur Patres: Sanguis Domini nostri Jesu Christi pretium totius mundi est, a quo pretio extranei sunt, qui aut delectati captivitate redimi noluerunt, aut post redemtionem ad eandem sunt servitutem reverti — Prosper. ad Capit. Gallor. sent. super 9. Sic Ecclesia nostra Anglicana, Artic. 2: Christus vere passus est, crucifixus, mortuus et sepultus, ut Patrem nobis reconciliaret, essetque hostia non tantum pro culpa originis, verum etiam pro omnibus actualibus hominum peccatis. Denique non possunt hoc diffiteri qui maxime hanc Christi mortem solent arctare. Reverendus et doctissimus Pareus in judicio suo de secundo hoc Remonstrantium articulo, quod transmisit ad Synodum Dordrechtanam, haec verba habet: Causa et materia passionis Christi fuit sensus sive sustinentia irae Dei, peccato non aliquorum hominum, sed universi generis humani concitatae, unde universitas peccati et irae Dei adversus illud a Christo toleratae efficitur; Universitas vero reconciliationis impetratae vel restitutae omnibus minime — Act. Synod. Dordrecht. pag. 217. Vis argumenti est, Qui voluit et ordinavit ut Christus Mediator sustineret iram Dei debitam peccatis non certarum personarum sed universi generis humani, ille voluit hanc passionem Christi esse remedium applicabile humano generi, hoc est, omnibus et singulis hominibus, et non solummodo singularibus quibusdam personis, relicta tamen sibi suprema potestate et omnimoda libertate dispensandi et applicandi hoc meritum infinitum juxta arcanum beneplacitum voluntatis suae.

Quicunque ex ordinatione Divina possunt vocari ut credant in Mediatorem, et qui credendo obtinere possunt vitam aeternam; illis mors Christi ex praevia ordinatione Dei est applicabilis ad salutem: Sed quilibet viator vocari potest ut credat in Mediatorem, et credendo ex pacto Evangelico obtinere potest vitam aeternam: Ergo mors Christi est cuilibet viatori applicabilis. Connexio Majoris inde patet, quod vocatio seria ad credendum praesupponit objectum paratum in quod credatur: et hoc ipsum posse salvari credendo innuit salutiferum objectum, id est, Mortem sive meritum Christi, esse ordinatum ut remedium applicabile illi cui sub conditione fidei tale beneficium promittitur. Si enim ille vocaretur ad fidem in Christum cui Christus non esset ex ordinatione Dei applicabilis; fides in falsum objectum, imo in nullum plane, quoad talem vocatum, postularetur. Perinde enim se res haberet atque si Evangelicus praedicator Daemonem aliquem humana specie indutum et inter homines versantem vocaret ad fidem in Christum, et promitteret illi, si crederet, vitam aeternam. Talis vocatio erronea esset ex parte vocantis, et inanis ex parte vocati, quia is vocatur ad credendum in Christum cui Christus ex ordinatione Dei non est applicabilis, et illi promittitur salus sub conditione, cui, etiamsi credere supponeretur, salus tamen denegatur ob defectum hostiae et pacti ad illum pertinentis. Non ita se res habet in ullo viatore: ergo fateri oportet mortem Christi sub conditionibus Evangelici pacti esse cuivis applicabilem.

Confirmata Majore, accedo ad Minorem; quae extra controversiam esse debet apud omnes orthodoxos. Nam quamvis Dei providentia non procuret ut omnibus et singulis innotescat Evangelium, et sic omnes ad Christum vocentur, tamen Deus ipse constituit ut Evangelium esset quiddam vere annunciabile omnibus, et praedicaretur omni creaturae. Si quis unus praedicator posset totum orbem obire, et omnes ac singulos mortales convenire, liceret illi cuivis homini Christum offerre, et sub conditione fidei salutem per Christum obtinendam annunciare et promittere. Sic enim loquitur ipse Apostolus, Rom. iii. 21, 22: Nunc absque lege justitia Dei patefacta est, comprobata testimonio legis et prophetarum; Justitia, inquam, Dei per fidem Jesu Christi in omnes et super omnes qui credunt: non enim est distinctio. Doctissimi Professores Belgici, in judicio suo exhibito Synodo Dordrechtanae hoc ipsum fatentur, Act. Synod. Dordr. p. 88: Fatémur, inquiunt, Meritum et valorem mortis Christi non tantum sufficere ad omnia hominum peccata, etiam maxima, expianda, sed etiam ad omnes Adami posteros, quamvis multo plures essent, servandos, modo id vera fide amplecterentur. At non sufficeret ad omnes servandos, etiamsi omnes crederent, nisi hoc posito, quod ordinatione Divina haec mors Christi sit constitutum remedium omnibus applicabile. Nega tu Christum pro aliquibus hominibus mortuum, et ego protinus inferam, Tales, etiamsi crederent, per mortem Christi salvari non posse. Quod a nonnullis huic argumento responderi solet, Deum non mandasse ministris ut annunciarent Christum mortuum esse pro singulis hominibus, sive ii credant sive non credant, sed pro solis credentibus et poenitentibus peccatoribus, ac proinde ex universalitate vocationis non posse demonstrari mortem Christi esse ex ordinatione Divina universale remedium cuivis applicabile, id mihi parum considerate dictum videtur. Nam fides hominum non prerequiritur ut conditio quae faciat Christum pro illis fuisse mortuum, sed quae faciat mortem Christi, ex Divina eudokia omnibus applicabilem, ipso actu singulis applicatam et fructuosam. Mors Christi fuit sacrificium ab origine mundi in acceptatione Divina stabilitum et hominibus ordinatum: nec posset quenquam juvare, si crederet, nisi fuisset pro illo oblata antequam crederet. Cum igitur annunciamus alicui, mortem Christi prodesse posse ei, si credat, praesumimus illi fuisse destinatam, ut applicabile priusquam credat.
english: Whoever, by undergoing death according to God’s ordination, sustained the penalty owed not only to the sins of certain singular persons but to the whole human race — his passion, by virtue of the same ordination, is applicable not only to certain and definite persons but to any individual of the human race. But Christ by dying sustained the penalty owed to the sins of the whole world. Therefore he willed his death to be, as it were, a universal cause of salvation applicable to all. Whoever denies the Major is bound to show why God willed his Son to bear the sins of the human race, if he did not will to institute in his death a cause at least applicable to the human race, even though an efficacious application does not follow in many. We can invent no other causes of this matter than that it pleased the divine goodness and wisdom to require from our Redeemer, and as it were to take into his own hands, a universal lytron applicable to all: (1) that in the application itself the liberty of the divine will, doing of its own what it wills, and a special eudokia toward the elect, might more appear; (2) that toward the non-elect, at least those called in the Church, he might show a specimen of great mercy; (3) that unbelievers might be convicted in their consciences that on Christ’s part a way of freeing them was not wanting, but that they failed themselves, according to Christ’s word ([[John 5:40 >> Bible:John 5:40]]): You will not come to me, that you may have life.

Let us now descend to the Minor, in which it is affirmed that Christ sustained the penalty owed to the sins of the human race. So the Scriptures speak ([[Isaiah 53:6 >> Bible:Isaiah 53:6]]): All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the Lord has made the iniquity of us all to meet upon him. So the Fathers speak: The blood of our Lord Jesus Christ is the price of the whole world, from which price those are strangers who either, delighted with captivity, refused to be redeemed, or after redemption returned to the same servitude (Prosper, on the Chapters of the Gauls, sentence on 9). So our Church of England, Article 2: Christ truly suffered, was crucified, dead, and buried, that he might reconcile the Father to us, and might be a sacrifice not only for original guilt but also for all actual sins of human beings. Finally, those who most tightly restrict this death of Christ cannot deny this. The reverend and most learned Pareus, in his judgment on this second Remonstrant article which he sent to the Synod of Dort, has these words: The cause and matter of Christ’s passion was the sense or endurance of the wrath of God stirred up by the sin not of some human beings but of the whole human race, whence is effected the universality of the sin and of the wrath of God against it endured by Christ; but the universality of a reconciliation obtained or restored for all, by no means (Acts of the Synod of Dort, p. 217). The force of the argument is: Whoever willed and ordained that Christ the Mediator should sustain the wrath of God owed to the sins not of certain persons but of the whole human race, that one willed this passion of Christ to be a remedy applicable to the human race — that is, to each and every human being, and not only to certain singular persons — the supreme power and entire liberty of dispensing and applying this infinite merit according to the secret good pleasure of his will being nonetheless left to himself.

Whoever by divine ordination can be called to believe in the Mediator, and who by believing can obtain eternal life — to those the death of Christ is applicable unto salvation by a prior ordination of God. But any wayfarer can be called to believe in the Mediator, and by believing can obtain eternal life according to the evangelical covenant. Therefore the death of Christ is applicable to any wayfarer. The connection of the Major is plain from this: that a serious call to believe presupposes an object prepared in which one may believe; and this very ability to be saved by believing intimates that the saving object — that is, the death or merit of Christ — has been ordained as a remedy applicable to the one to whom such a benefit is promised under the condition of faith. For if someone were called to faith in Christ to whom Christ was not applicable by God’s ordination, faith would be demanded in a false object — indeed in none at all — as regards such a called person. The matter would stand just as if an evangelical preacher should call some demon clothed in human appearance and dwelling among human beings to faith in Christ, and should promise him eternal life if he believed. Such a call would be erroneous on the caller’s part and empty on the called person’s part, because he is called to believe in Christ to whom Christ is not applicable by God’s ordination, and salvation is promised to him under a condition to whom, even if he were supposed to believe, salvation is nonetheless denied for want of a sacrifice and covenant pertaining to him. The matter does not stand so with any wayfarer: therefore it must be confessed that the death of Christ under the conditions of the evangelical covenant is applicable to anyone.

The Major being confirmed, I come to the Minor, which ought to be beyond controversy among all the orthodox. For although God’s providence does not bring it about that the Gospel becomes known to each and every person, and thus that all are called to Christ, yet God himself constituted that the Gospel should be something truly announceable to all, and should be preached to every creature. If one preacher could go through the whole world and meet each and every mortal, it would be lawful for him to offer Christ to any human being, and under the condition of faith to announce and promise salvation to be obtained through Christ. For so the Apostle himself speaks ([[Romans 3:21-22 >> Bible:Romans 3:21-22]]): But now apart from the law the righteousness of God has been manifested, attested by the law and the prophets — the righteousness of God, I say, through faith in Jesus Christ unto all and upon all who believe; for there is no distinction. The most learned Belgian Professors, in the judgment they exhibited to the Synod of Dort, confess this very thing (Acts of the Synod of Dort, p. 88): We confess, they say, that the merit and value of Christ’s death suffice not only to expiate all sins of human beings, even the greatest, but also to save all the posterity of Adam, even if they were far more numerous, provided they embraced it with true faith. But it would not suffice to save all, even if all believed, unless this be posited: that by divine ordination this death of Christ is a constituted remedy applicable to all. Deny that Christ died for some human beings, and I will at once infer that such persons, even if they believed, could not be saved through the death of Christ. What is commonly answered to this argument by some — that God did not command ministers to announce that Christ died for individual human beings whether they believe or not, but for believing and penitent sinners alone, and therefore that from the universality of the call it cannot be demonstrated that the death of Christ is by divine ordination a universal remedy applicable to anyone — seems to me said with too little consideration. For the faith of human beings is not presupposed as a condition that makes Christ to have died for them, but as a condition that makes the death of Christ — already applicable to all by the divine eudokia — in fact applied to individuals and fruitful. The death of Christ was a sacrifice established in the divine acceptation from the beginning of the world and ordained for human beings; nor could it help anyone, if he believed, unless it had been offered for him before he believed. When therefore we announce to someone that the death of Christ can profit him if he believes, we presume that it was destined for him as applicable before he believes.

source_text: Si omnes mortales, statim atque illis innotescit doctrina Evangelii de Christo redemtore mortem ob peccata hominum sustinente, teneantur ad gratitudinem et obsequium praestandum ipsi Christo, tum certum est hoc opus Redemtoris seipsum in hostiam Deo offerentis considerandum ut beneficium omnibus promiscue applicabile: Nulla enim causa est cur dicamus illos teneri ad gratitudinem, aut ad quaevis obsequia praestanda, ratione mortis Christi, qui ab illo beneficio sunt omnibus modis exclusissimi: At Apostolus testatur quosvis homines hoc ipso argumento excitari posse ad obedientiam. Nam quibusvis hominibus vere dici potest post patefactum illis hoc mysterium mortis Christi quod habetur 1 Cor. vi. 20. Empti estis pretio: glorificate Deum in corpore vestro et spiritu vestro. Item et illud 2 Cor. v. 15. Pro omnibus mortuus est, ut qui vivant posthac non sibi vivant, sed ei qui ipsis mortuus est, et resurrexit. Nisi Christi mors remedium universis applicabile intelligatur, semper erit incertum et saepe falsum illud fundamentum cui ministri Evangelici hujusmodi hortationes superstruunt. Semper incertum; quia hominibus constare non potest quinam sunt electi. Saepe falsum; quoties nimirum adhibetur non-electis, qui ex hoc titulo redemtionis non tenentur vivere Christo, nisi praesupponatur hostiam illam a Christo oblatam pro redemtione mundi esse illis applicabilem. Imo ipse Christus jure mortis suae non posset in omnes et singulos sibi vendicare supremam quandam dominationem, nisi mors ejus juxta ordinationem Dei esset meritum omnibus applicabile ad salutem. Cum igitur ad hoc Christus mortuus fuerit et revixerit, ut et vivis et mortuis dominetur, Rom. xiv. 9. debemus, saltem quoad jus et potestatem salutiferae applicationis, ejus mortem ad omnes extendere: quamvis Spiritus Christi (qui spirat ubi vult) det hominibus facultatem et voluntatem applicandi, atque ipsum adeo fructum mortis applicatae, ex specialis misericordiae decreto.
english: If all mortals, as soon as the doctrine of the Gospel concerning Christ the Redeemer sustaining death for the sins of human beings becomes known to them, are bound to render gratitude and obedience to Christ himself, then it is certain that this work of the Redeemer offering himself as a sacrifice to God is to be considered as a benefit applicable promiscuously to all. For there is no cause why we should say that those are bound to gratitude, or to any acts of obedience whatever, by reason of the death of Christ, who are in every way most shut out from that benefit. Yet the Apostle testifies that any human beings whatever can be stirred to obedience by this very argument. For to any human beings whatever it can truly be said, after this mystery of Christ’s death has been made known to them, what is found in ([[1 Corinthians 6:20 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 6:20]]): You were bought with a price; glorify God in your body and in your spirit. Likewise also ([[2 Corinthians 5:15 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 5:15]]): He died for all, that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and rose again.

Unless the death of Christ is understood as a remedy applicable to all, that foundation on which evangelical ministers build exhortations of this kind will always be uncertain and often false. Always uncertain, because it cannot be clear to human beings who the elect are. Often false, whenever it is applied to the non-elect, who on this title of redemption are not bound to live to Christ unless it be presupposed that that sacrifice offered by Christ for the redemption of the world is applicable to them. Indeed Christ himself could not by right of his death claim for himself a certain supreme lordship over each and every person, unless his death, according to God’s ordination, were a merit applicable to all unto salvation. Since therefore Christ died and lived again for this, that he might be Lord both of the living and of the dead ([[Romans 14:9 >> Bible:Romans 14:9]]), we ought, at least as to the right and power of saving application, to extend his death to all — although the Spirit of Christ (who breathes where he wills) gives to human beings the faculty and will to apply, and even the very fruit of the death applied, by a decree of special mercy.

source_text:
Illud opus quod vere et merito, simulac transactum intelligitur inter Deum Patrem et Filium, dat Christo nomen Redemtoris mundi, et Servatoris mundi, agnoscendum est ut universalis causa salutis, vel remedium universale toti humano generi applicabile: sed tale fuit opus obedientiae Christi usque ad mortem Crucis; Ergo, etc. Major inde confirmatur quod ex parte ipsius pretii persoluti Christus esset tantum Redemtor et Servator particularis, si pretium persolutum juxta ordinationem Dei non esset applicabile quibusvis humani generis individuis. Nos igitur qui nomen et titulum Redemtoris et Servatoris mundi Christo concedimus, id simul concedere debemus; hanc redemtionem, unde ita denominatur, esse solutionem pretii debiti pro liberatione humani generis; quod apud Deum hactenus valet, ut nullam aliam satisfactionem possit requirere ad quemvis hominem sibi reconciliandum; et nobis omnibus eatenus profit, ut possit quivis peccator liberari, modo in hunc Redemtorem credat, et (quod in remediis fieri semper oportet) hanc salutarem medicinam per fidem sibi applicet. Hoc sensu vere dicimus Christum pro omnibus hominibus mortuum, et hanc mortem Christi, sive redemtionem morte ejus acquisitam, esse meritum omnibus et singulis hominibus applicabile, quod de Angelis lapsis nullo modo affirmari potest. Est igitur Redemtor et Servator omnium hominum Christus Jesus causaliter, ut Schola loquitur, id est, instituendo et suppeditando causam sufficientem et ordinatam atque acceptatam a Deo ad expianda peccata quorumcunque qui hoc remedio uti volunt. Hoc sufficit ad fundandum titulum universalis Servatoris et Redemtoris, quamvis voluntas credendi non donetur omnibus.

Jam ad Minorem veniamus, quae tam perspicua est ut operosa probatione non egeat. Scripturae, respiciendo ad hanc mortem Christi omnibus applicabilem, appellant illum Servatorem mundi, Johann. iv. 42: Hic est vere Servator ille mundi Christus. Vocant ipsam Christi mortem lytron datum pro redemtione omnium, 1 Tim. ii. 6. propitiationem pro peccatis totius mundi, 1 Johann. ii. 2. Catholica etiam Ecclesia in publicis suis precibus Christum mundi Redemtorem semper indigitavit. Ne autem quis torqueat hujusmodi appellationes in illum sensum, quasi Christus Redemtor mundi diceretur, quia electos per totum mundum dispersos efficaciter redimit, illud ad extremum addo, et Patres et scriptores modernos sensu a nobis posito Christum mundi Redemtorem asseruisse; nimirum, quod ejus mors sit lytron ex ordinatione Dei omnibus et singulis hominibus applicabile. Huc faciunt illa Prosperi verba, Ad Object. Vincentian. Resp. 1. Propter unam omnium naturam et unam omnium causam a Domino nostro in veritate susceptam, recte omnes dicuntur redemti, et tamen non omnes a captivitate sunt eruti, etc. Et paulo post, Poculum immortalitatis quod confectum est de infirmitate nostra et virtute Divina habet quidem in se ut omnibus prosit: sed si non bibitur, non medetur. Eodem spectant et illa Musculi a nobis ante citata, Loc. Comm. pag. 151. Scimus non omnes redemtionis hujus fieri participes: verum illorum perditio qui non servantur, haudquaquam impedit quo minus universalis vocetur redemtio. Nam quod illam homines reprobi non accipiant, neque defectu sit gratiae Dei, neque justum est ut illa propter Filios perditionis gloriam ac titulum universalis redemtionis amittat, cum sit parata cunctis, et omnes ad illam vocentur. Ex quibus omnibus illud elucet, Christum recte dici Redemtorem et Servatorem mundi, quod toti humano generi apportaverit remedium ad salutem singulorum procurandam applicabile.
english: That work which truly and by merit, as soon as it is understood to have been transacted between God the Father and the Son, gives Christ the name Redeemer of the world and Savior of the world, must be acknowledged as a universal cause of salvation, or a universal remedy applicable to the whole human race. But such was the work of Christ’s obedience unto the death of the cross. Therefore, etc. The Major is confirmed from this: that on the side of the price itself paid, Christ would be only a particular Redeemer and Savior if the price paid were not, by God’s ordination, applicable to any individuals of the human race whatever. We therefore who grant to Christ the name and title of Redeemer and Savior of the world must at the same time grant this: that this redemption, from which he is so named, is the payment of the price owed for the liberation of the human race — a payment which so far avails with God that he can require no other satisfaction for reconciling any human being to himself; and which so far profits us all that any sinner can be freed, provided he believes in this Redeemer and (as must always be done with remedies) applies this saving medicine to himself by faith. In this sense we truly say that Christ died for all human beings, and that this death of Christ, or the redemption acquired by his death, is a merit applicable to each and every human being — which can in no way be affirmed of the fallen angels. Christ Jesus is therefore Redeemer and Savior of all human beings causally, as the Schools speak: that is, by instituting and supplying a cause sufficient and ordained and accepted by God for expiating the sins of whoever will use this remedy. This suffices to found the title of universal Savior and Redeemer, even though the will to believe is not given to all.

We now come to the Minor, which is so clear that it does not need laborious proof. The Scriptures, looking to this death of Christ applicable to all, call him the Savior of the world ([[John 4:42 >> Bible:John 4:42]]): This is truly the Christ, the Savior of the world. They call the death of Christ itself a lytron given for the redemption of all ([[1 Timothy 2:6 >> Bible:1 Timothy 2:6]]), a propitiation for the sins of the whole world ([[1 John 2:2 >> Bible:1 John 2:2]]). The Catholic Church also in her public prayers has always named Christ the Redeemer of the world. But lest anyone twist appellations of this kind into the sense that Christ would be called Redeemer of the world because he efficaciously redeems the elect scattered through the whole world, I add at the end that both the Fathers and modern writers have asserted Christ to be Redeemer of the world in the sense we have set down — namely, that his death is a lytron applicable by God’s ordination to each and every human being. Here belong those words of Prosper, answering Vincent’s objection, Response 1: On account of the one nature of all and the one cause of all truly assumed by our Lord, all are rightly said to be redeemed, and yet not all have been delivered from captivity, etc. And a little later: The cup of immortality compounded of our infirmity and the divine power has indeed in itself what would profit all; but if it is not drunk, it does not heal. The same is the aim of those words of Musculus already cited by us (Common Places, p. 151): We know that not all become partakers of this redemption; yet the perdition of those who are not saved by no means hinders its being called a universal redemption. For that reprobate human beings do not receive it is neither a defect of the grace of God, nor is it just that on account of the sons of perdition it should lose the glory and title of a universal redemption, since it is prepared for all and all are called to it. From all of which it is clear that Christ is rightly called Redeemer and Savior of the world, because he brought to the whole human race a remedy applicable unto procuring the salvation of individuals.

source_text:
Si fuit consilium et voluntas Dei ut Christus moriendo lytron sibi in manus traderet absolutissimum, perfectissimum et sufficientissimum, non modo pro illis liberandis qui Dei beneficio credunt, et sic quoad eventum salvantur, sed etiam pro illis qui suo vitio manent increduli, et sic quoad eventum damnantur, tum fatendum est, hanc mortem Christi esse remedium ex natura rei et ordinatione Dei omnibus applicabile: At tale fuit Dei consilium, talis voluntas: Quod evincitur ex promissionibus divinis, quae ejus voluntatem nobis indicant. Promisit enim Deus salutem sub conditione fidei et poenitentiae etiam illis qui conditiones hasce nunquam sunt praestituri. Sic ipsi Caino, si resipiscat, promittitur remissio, Gen. iv. 7. Quae salus sive remissio peccatorum sub conditione personae tali promissa clare arguit causam salutis eidem personae esse paratam et sub dicta conditione applicabilem. Idem evincitur ex eo, quod Deus in opere redemtionis ita consilium suum instituerit, ut nemo mortalium vere conqueri possit se defectu hostiae expiatoriae periisse. At hostiam sibi defuisse non minus vere potest affirmare is cui mors Christi non est remedium ad salutem ex Dei voluntate applicabile, quam Angeli mali, quibus sub nulla conditione mors Christi ordinatur. Atque hoc est illud consilium quod sprevisse dicuntur Pharisaei, Luc. vii. 30.

Si secundum ordinem et naturam ipsarum rerum, atque considerationis nostrae, mors et meritum Christi ponendum est ut quiddam prius a Deo ordinatum et destinatum in bonum humani generis, quam fides cuiquam destinata intelligatur, tum necesse est illud cogitare ut causam salutis omnibus applicabilem, priusquam huic et illi applicata aut infallibiliter applicanda statuatur. Ratio consecutionis haec est: Quod Christi mors sive meritum nemini applicatum aut applicandum intelligitur, donec fides eidem concessa aut concedenda concipitur: Et e contra, cuivis applicabilis consideratur mors Christi, priusquam fides illi in perpetuum denegata aut deneganda concipitur. Jam adjungo Minorem, nempe mortem Christi sive meritum ejus infinitum poni debere, ut quiddam prius stabilitum et destinatum hominibus, quam fides hisce aut illis singularibus personis destinetur. Quod patet primo, quia mors sive meritum Christi est objectum Fidei: quorsum vero destinaret Petro aut Paulo donare fidem, nisi prius ordinasset salutis remedium mediante fide cuivis applicabile? Porro, fides, sicuti et reliqua omnia dona salutaria, confertur hominibus propter Christum, et ex merito Christi: praecedit itaque in ordine decretorum Divinorum mors Christi fidem cujuscunque Christiani. Huc faciunt illa Theologorum Palatinorum verba, in judicio suo Dordrechtano exhibito, Act. Synod. Dordrecht. pag. 88. Fides electorum mortem Christi non antecedit sed sequitur, quia mors illa est causa fidei, qua propter Christum donantur electi, et objectum ejus, quod ipsa intuetur et complectitur. Denique universis hominibus in primo Adamo perditis, in secundi Adami morte salus parabilis decernitur priusquam quibus efficaciter et infallibiliter danda, quibus non danda sit, decernatur. Fatendum est igitur Mediatorem Jesum Christum, cum morte et infinito meritorum suorum thesauro, esse ex ordinatione Dei toti humano generi ad salutem applicabilem, quamvis interveniat liberrimum, justissimum, occultissimum Dei beneplacitum, juxta quod fidem (qua mediante fiat applicatio) certis personis infallibiliter donandam, aliis minime donandam statuat. Cur autem in dispensando thesauro meritorum Christi, omnibus et singulis sufficiente et applicabili, tam inaequaliter agat cum aequalibus, nos quia scire non possumus, quaerere non debemus, sed cum Apostolo, in arcana Dei voluntate acquiescere, qui cujus vult miseretur, et quem vult indurat, Rom. ix. 18. cui nemo prior dedit, ut ex debito ei reddere teneatur. Rom. xi. 35.
english: If it was the counsel and will of God that Christ by dying should deliver into his hands a lytron most absolute, most perfect, and most sufficient, not only for freeing those who by God’s benefit believe and so are saved as to the event, but also for those who by their own fault remain unbelieving and so are damned as to the event, then it must be confessed that this death of Christ is a remedy applicable to all by the nature of the thing and by God’s ordination. And such was God’s counsel, such his will — which is proved from the divine promises that indicate his will to us. For God promised salvation under the condition of faith and repentance even to those who will never perform these conditions. So to Cain himself, if he repent, remission is promised ([[Genesis 4:7 >> Bible:Genesis 4:7]]). Which salvation, or remission of sins, promised under condition to such a person, clearly argues that a cause of salvation was prepared for that same person and is applicable under the said condition. The same is proved from this: that God so ordered his counsel in the work of redemption that no mortal can truly complain that he perished for want of an expiatory sacrifice. Yet he to whom the death of Christ is not a remedy applicable unto salvation by God’s will can no less truly affirm that a sacrifice was wanting to him than can the evil angels, for whom the death of Christ is ordained under no condition. And this is that counsel which the Pharisees are said to have despised ([[Luke 7:30 >> Bible:Luke 7:30]]).

If according to the order and nature of the things themselves, and of our consideration, the death and merit of Christ must be posited as something first ordained and destined by God for the good of the human race before faith is understood to be destined for anyone, then it is necessary to think of it as a cause of salvation applicable to all before it is stated as applied, or to be applied infallibly, to this one and that. The reason of the consequence is this: that the death or merit of Christ is understood as applied or to be applied to no one until faith is conceived as granted or to be granted to him; and on the contrary, the death of Christ is considered applicable to anyone before faith is conceived as denied or to be denied to him forever. I now add the Minor: namely, that the death of Christ, or his infinite merit, must be posited as something first established and destined for human beings before faith is destined for these or those singular persons. This is plain, first, because the death or merit of Christ is the object of faith: to what end would he destine to give faith to Peter or to Paul unless he had first ordained a remedy of salvation applicable to anyone through the medium of faith? Further, faith, like all other saving gifts, is conferred on human beings on account of Christ and from the merit of Christ; therefore in the order of the divine decrees the death of Christ precedes the faith of every Christian. Here belong those words of the Palatine theologians in the judgment they exhibited at Dort (Acts of the Synod of Dort, p. 88): The faith of the elect does not precede but follows the death of Christ, because that death is the cause of the faith by which the elect are given on account of Christ, and its object, which faith itself looks upon and embraces. Finally, for all human beings lost in the first Adam, a obtainable salvation is decreed in the death of the second Adam before it is decreed to whom it is to be given efficaciously and infallibly, and to whom it is not to be given. It must therefore be confessed that the Mediator Jesus Christ, with his death and the infinite treasury of his merits, is by God’s ordination applicable to the whole human race unto salvation, although there intervene the freest, most just, and most hidden good pleasure of God, according to which he decrees that faith (by whose medium application is made) is to be given infallibly to certain persons and by no means to others. But why, in dispensing the treasury of Christ’s merits — sufficient and applicable to each and every person — he deals so unequally with equals, we ought not to ask, because we cannot know, but with the Apostle to rest in the secret will of God, who has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens ([[Romans 9:18 >> Bible:Romans 9:18]]); to whom no one has first given, that he should be bound to repay him as a debt ([[Romans 11:35 >> Bible:Romans 11:35]]).

source_text: Ultima ratio petitur ex collatione duplicis foederis, et secundum illud, duplicis ordinationis hominum ad salutem. Sicut igitur in foedere naturae, quod cum Adamo in ipsa creatione pactum intelligitur, salus fuit Adamo et omnibus ejus posteris parabilis, sub conditione obedientiae legi naturae et expresso Dei mandato praestandae, sic in foedere gratiae, quod in Mediatoris sanguine sancitum est, salus etiam omnibus hominibus parabilis intelligitur sub conditione in Evangelio publicata, scilicet, fidei in hunc mediatorem, qui satisfecit pro peccatis humani generis. Porro, sicut in primo foedere Deus, qui ordinavit salutem ut parabilem Adamo et posteris ejus, non tamen praedestinavit ut vel ipse Adamus, vel ullus ex posteris ejus per illud foedus reapse salvaretur, ita Deus, qui in secundo foedere ordinavit salutem ut omnibus parabilem sub conditione fidei, non tamen praedestinavit fidem hanc dare omnibus et singulis, qui infallibiliter salutem consequerentur. Ne tamen difflueret sanguis Filii Dei, et vitio humani arbitrii idem eveniret in secundo foedere quod eveniret in primo, nempe, ut ejus beneficio nemo frueretur, agitavit Deus apud se altius et secretius consilium, atque statuit ex mera et speciali misericordia quibusdam donare ut praedictam fidei conditionem et possint et velint implere, imo ut de facto infallibiliter impleant. Jam vero sicuti injurius esset in Deum, qui negaret salutem fuisse a Deo ordinatam, ut parabilem Adamo et posteris ejus sub foedere naturae, quamvis juxta illud foedus nemo fuit factus salutis compos, ita in Christum magis injurius est, qui negat mortem ejus a Deo fuisse ordinatam, ut remedium salutis sub conditione foederis novi applicabile omnibus, quamvis multi inde salutem non consequantur. Ipse Deus dedit mundo hoc remedium omnibus et singulis applicabile: concedat mundus Deo libertatem illud applicandi vel non applicandi, prout ejus sapientiae, misericordiae ac justitiae visum fuerit. Qui hoc modo de morte Christi sentiunt, illam communem Dei philanthropian, quam Scriptura testatur, non e medio tollunt: et tamen simul tuentur, quotquot merito mortis Christi servantur, speciali et immerita gratia fuisse servatos; quotquot non servantur, propria infidelitate aut saltem culpa periisse. Plures rationes ad corroborandam sententiam nostram congerere superflue. Quod in contrarium objici solet jam audiamus.
english: The last reason is drawn from a comparison of the twofold covenant, and according to it of the twofold ordination of human beings unto salvation. As therefore in the covenant of nature, which is understood as made with Adam in the very creation, salvation was obtainable for Adam and all his posterity under the condition of obedience to be rendered to the law of nature and to the express command of God, so in the covenant of grace, which was sanctioned in the blood of the Mediator, salvation is understood as obtainable for all human beings also under the condition published in the Gospel — namely, faith in this Mediator who satisfied for the sins of the human race. Further, as in the first covenant God, who ordained salvation as obtainable for Adam and his posterity, nevertheless did not predestine that either Adam himself or any of his posterity should in fact be saved through that covenant, so God, who in the second covenant ordained salvation as obtainable for all under the condition of faith, nevertheless did not predestine to give this faith to each and every person who would infallibly obtain salvation.

Yet lest the blood of the Son of God should flow away, and by the fault of human choice the same should happen in the second covenant that had happened in the first — namely, that no one should enjoy its benefit — God stirred within himself a higher and more secret counsel, and decreed out of mere and special mercy to give to some that they both can and will fulfill the aforesaid condition of faith, indeed that they in fact fulfill it infallibly. Now just as he would be injurious to God who should deny that salvation was ordained by God as obtainable for Adam and his posterity under the covenant of nature, even though according to that covenant no one was made partaker of salvation, so he is more injurious to Christ who denies that his death was ordained by God as a remedy of salvation applicable to all under the condition of the new covenant, even though many do not obtain salvation from it. God himself gave to the world this remedy applicable to each and every person: let the world grant God the liberty of applying it or not applying it, as shall seem good to his wisdom, mercy, and justice. Those who think of the death of Christ in this way do not take out of the midst that common philanthropy of God which Scripture testifies; and yet they at the same time maintain that as many as are saved by the merit of Christ’s death have been saved by special and unmerited grace, and that as many as are not saved have perished by their own unbelief or at least by their own fault. It is superfluous to heap up more reasons for corroborating our opinion. What is customarily objected on the contrary side let us now hear.

source_text:
CAPUT III. Satisfit objectionibus adversariorum.

Priusquam ea diluamus quae in contrariam partem obtendi possunt, illud praemonendum est, nos haud agere illorum causam qui statuunt Christum morte sua omnibus et singulis hominibus impetravisse remissionem peccatorum, reconciliationem cum Deo, et statum salutis. Sic Borreus apud Arminium sentire videtur, qui hoc fundamento nixus asserit omnes omnium gentium infantes morientes sine peccatis actualibus salvos esse, quia Deus universum genus humanum in reconciliationis gratiam assumpserit. Opinatur ergo ipso sacrificio mortis Christi totum humanum genus in statu salutis collocari, a quo si non exciderint, salutem indubie obtinebunt. Eundem errorem Hubero et Puccio multi adscribunt. Nostra autem defensio est; non quidem hac morte Christi salutem esse de facto impetratam omnibus et singulis, aut omnes et singulos ejus beneficio esse in gratiam receptos, et in talem statum repositos, in quo si perseverint, vitam aeternam possiderent; sed hanc mortem Christi esse, ex Divinae voluntatis decreto, remedium toti humano generi, vel cuivis humani generis individuo, applicabile ad salutem, quamvis in ipsa applicatione procuranda et efficienda Deus quorundam specialiter misereatur, quorundam minime. Hanc sententiam aliquot argumentis stabilitam accepistis: jam ab objectionibus quae in contrariam partem afferri possunt eam vindicemus.
english: Before we dissolve those things which can be urged on the contrary side, this is to be premised: we are by no means pleading the cause of those who maintain that Christ by his death obtained for all and each human being the remission of sins, reconciliation with God, and a state of salvation. So Borreus seems to think in Arminius, who, resting on this foundation, asserts that all infants of all nations dying without actual sins are saved, because God took the whole human race into the grace of reconciliation. He therefore opines that by the very sacrifice of Christ's death the whole human race is placed in a state of salvation, from which if they do not fall away they will without doubt obtain salvation. Many ascribe the same error to Huber and Puccius. But our defense is this: not indeed that by this death of Christ salvation has in fact been obtained for all and each, or that all and each have by its benefit been received into grace and set in such a state that if they persevered they would possess eternal life; but that this death of Christ is, by the decree of the Divine will, a remedy applicable to the whole human race, or to any individual of the human race, unto salvation — although in procuring and effecting the application itself God specially has mercy on some and not on others. You have received this opinion established by several arguments: now let us vindicate it from the objections which can be brought on the contrary side.

source_text:
Obj. 1. Primum igitur objici potest, eo tempore quo Christus mortem oppetebat, multos fuisse gehennae adjudicatos et in inferno cruciatos: ab inferno autem nulla redemtio est. Quomodo igitur tueri possumus Christi mortem fuisse hisce damnatis hominibus unquam ullo modo applicabilem? Hoc argumento permoti nonnulli statuerunt, innumerabilem illam multitudinem impiorum qui fuerunt ab initio mundi usque ad adventum Christi, quique propter suam impietatem in infernum conjecti fuerunt, ante sacrificium Christi in cruce oblatum non plus juris habuisse in redemtionis beneficium quam ipsos Diabolos. Sic loquuntur Lugdunenses Patres in scripto quodam quod exstat Tom. 9. Biblioth. Patrum: Sicut pro impiis et damnatis angelis nullatenus Dominus Jesus Christus dicendus est passus; ita pro istis impiis et damnatis hominibus absit ut omnia passus esse credatur.

Sol. Sed respondeo, Quando affirmamus Christi mortem ex ordinatione Dei et natura rei esse remedium cuivis homini applicabile, non spectare nos solummodo externam passionem Christi praestituto temporis momento toleratam, sed aeternam virtutem mortis Christi quovis saeculo hominibus salutiferam. Christus enim quoad acceptationem Dei fuit Agnus occisus ab origine mundi: et efficacia hujus sacrificii propitiatorii tam extendere se potuit ad illos qui vixerunt ante Christum passum, quam ad nos qui vivimus post ejus passionem. Si illud igitur tantum volunt, temporali morte Christi non potuisse eos sublevari, qui ante mortem ejus irrevocabili decreto fuerunt poenis infernalibus adjudicati, nos idem confitemur; quia jam desierunt esse viatores, id est, poenitentiae et fidei capaces: sed si ultra contendere velint, virtutem aeternam mortis Christi non fuisse talibus applicabilem dum viverent, quia Christi passio non magis ad eos spectavit, quam ad impios et damnatos angelos, id nos pernegamus. Nam de Caino, Esavo, imo de quovis homine ante Christum passum mortuo vere dici potest, illum virtute sacrificii per Messiam offerendi a peccatis suis absolvi et servari potuisse, si in eundem credidisset: quod de angelis damnatis itidem dici nequit; quia universale pactum salutis sub conditione fidei universum genus humanum complectitur, angelos lapsos non complectitur. Est itaque observatione dignum, Deum noluisse mortem Christi sive applicatam sive sub conditione quacunque applicabilem ulli lapsorum angelorum — ad hosce ergo universos pariter et ex aequo se habuit Deus: at non ex aequo ad homines; nam quoad hosce, licet statuerit et declaraverit mortem Filii sui sub conditione fidei esse cuivis applicabilem, tamen non decrevit specialis misericordiae beneficio illam ex aequo cuivis reddere applicatam. Non negamus itaque, quod manifestum est, discrimen scilicet inter Daemones et Homines in eo situm, quod ex ordinatione Dei mors Christi sit quiddam ordinatum et applicabile hominibus; sed neque ordinatum neque applicabile daemonibus; licet post hanc vitam hominibus in inferno constitutis nulla ulterius reliqua sit possibilitas applicationis. Vitiosa etenim est haec consequentia: Christi mors non fuit applicabilis damnatis post illorum damnationem; Ergo nunquam et nullatenus fuit illis applicabilis.
english: Obj. 1. First, then, it can be objected that at the time when Christ underwent death many had already been adjudged to Gehenna and were being tormented in hell; and from hell there is no redemption. How then can we maintain that Christ's death was ever in any way applicable to these damned human beings? Moved by this argument some have held that that innumerable multitude of the impious who lived from the beginning of the world until Christ's coming, and who for their impiety were cast into hell, before Christ's sacrifice offered on the cross had no more right to the benefit of redemption than the Devils themselves. So the Lyons Fathers speak in a certain writing which stands in Tom. 9 of the Bibliotheca Patrum: Just as the Lord Jesus Christ is in no way to be said to have suffered for the impious and damned angels, so far be it that he be believed to have suffered all things for those impious and damned human beings.

Sol. But I reply: when we affirm that Christ's death, by God's ordination and by the nature of the thing, is a remedy applicable to any human being, we are not looking only at the external passion of Christ endured at a fixed moment of time, but at the eternal virtue of Christ's death, salutary to human beings in every age. For Christ, as to God's acceptance, was the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world; and the efficacy of this propitiatory sacrifice could extend itself as much to those who lived before Christ suffered as to us who live after his passion. If therefore they mean only this — that by Christ's temporal death those could not be relieved who before his death had by an irrevocable decree been adjudged to infernal punishments — we confess the same; because they have already ceased to be wayfarers, that is, capable of repentance and faith. But if they wish to contend further that the eternal virtue of Christ's death was not applicable to such while they lived, because Christ's passion looked no more to them than to the impious and damned angels, that we utterly deny. For of Cain, of Esau, indeed of any human being who died before Christ suffered, it can truly be said that by the virtue of the sacrifice to be offered through the Messiah he could have been absolved from his sins and saved, if he had believed in the same — which cannot likewise be said of the damned angels; because the universal covenant of salvation under the condition of faith embraces the whole human race and does not embrace the fallen angels. It is therefore worthy of observation that God willed Christ's death, whether applied or under whatever condition applicable, for none of the fallen angels — toward these, therefore, God held himself equally and alike; but not equally toward human beings. For as to these, although he established and declared that the death of his Son under the condition of faith is applicable to any, yet he did not decree by the benefit of special mercy to render it equally applied to any. We do not therefore deny what is manifest — the difference between Demons and Human beings, namely that by God's ordination Christ's death is something ordained and applicable to human beings, but neither ordained nor applicable to demons — although after this life, for human beings constituted in hell, no further possibility of application remains. For this consequence is vicious: Christ's death was not applicable to the damned after their damnation; therefore it was never and in no way applicable to them.

source_text:
Obj. 2. Qui ponunt Christi mortem ex ordinatione Dei omnibus et singulis applicabilem, eadem opera statuunt Deum providisse multis hominibus remedium quod praescit nunquam illis profuturum: Sciebat etenim Deus neminem reproborum hoc sanguinis Christi pharmaco sanandum et a morte aeterna liberandum; Quorsum igitur ordinaret tam pretiosum remedium etiam illis applicabile, quibus illud nunquam applicatum iri certissimum fuit?

Sol. Non inficias eo, ex nostra sententia illud recte sequi, remedium hoc, etiam ipso Deo ita ordinante et statuente, esse applicabile innumeris hominibus, quibus de facto nunquam applicabitur. Nego igitur aliquid falsi aut incommodi, hoc concesso, posse inde deduci. Imo manifestum est, angelis hominibusque multa beneficia a Deo provisa fuisse, addo etiam, et collata aliquando, atque ad finem certum debite ordinata, quae Deus interim sciebat nunquam illis profutura, neque ad producendum talem finem valitura. Dona illa eximia quae angelis apostatis in prima sua creatione collata fuerunt, erant a Deo debite ordinata ad firmam et constantem obedientiam in illis pariendam, atque ad beatitudinem eorundem procurandam; sciebat tamen Deus illos fore rebelles, atque haec dona nunquam adhibituris ad illius boni consecutionem cui erant destinata. Idem de Adamo integro dici potest, quem Deus scientia et sanctitate instruxit, quemque monitis suis praemunivit ad illum in officio continendum abunde sufficientibus; sciens interim haec omnia, quae erant applicabilia ad obedientiam et felicitatem ejus promovendam, nunquam iri applicata. Non est ergo alienum a Divina sapientia statuere et ordinare media ad finem aliquem applicabilia, licet intelligat interveniente aliquo obstaculo, quod ipse removere non decrevit, ipsam applicationem fore impediendam. Huc afferri potest illud Aquinatis, Quaest. disp. de Praedest., ubi discrimen ponit inter providentiam communiter sumptam et praedestinationem, quae est specialis pars providentiae: Providentia, inquit ille, ordinem in finem respicit tantum; praedestinatio respicit exitum vel eventum ordinis. Quae per providentiam illam communiorem ad finem ordinantur non semper finem consequuntur: at quae per praedestinationem singularem ordinantur, semper consequuntur. Sicuti ergo Deus per providentiam illam latiorem intelligitur multa remedia corporalia ad corporales quoscunque morbos a quibuscunque depellendos applicabilia providisse, quae tamen hisce aut illis singularibus personis non decrevit infallibiliter applicanda; ita et nos affirmamus Deum ex philanthropia et providentia illa communiori sanguinem Filii sui providisse et ordinasse ut remedium ad quorumcunque hominum peccata expianda applicabile, licet ex praedestinatione singulari non decreverit illud omnibus et singulis reddere applicatum. Sed quorsum ordinatur ut applicabile omnibus quod non intenditur omnibus infallibiliter applicandum? Respondeo, Ut hinc eluceat magis libertas, misericordia, justitia Divina, dum illud remedium quod ex Dei ordinatione est cuivis applicabile ad salutem, applicetur tamen solummodo certis hominibus, Deo eorundem specialiter miserante; non applicetur aliis, Deo id permittente, et propria illorum malitia id promerente.
english: Obj. 2. Those who set Christ's death, by God's ordination, as applicable to all and each, by the same stroke maintain that God provided for many human beings a remedy which he foresaw would never profit them. For God knew that none of the reprobate would be healed by this medicine of Christ's blood and freed from eternal death; to what end, then, would he ordain so precious a remedy as applicable even to those to whom it was most certain it would never be applied?

Sol. I do not deny that from our opinion it rightly follows that this remedy, even with God himself so ordaining and establishing it, is applicable to innumerable human beings to whom in fact it will never be applied. I deny, therefore, that anything false or inconvenient can, this being granted, be deduced from it. Indeed it is manifest that many benefits were provided by God for angels and human beings — I add also, and sometimes conferred, and duly ordained to a certain end — which God meanwhile knew would never profit them, nor avail to produce such an end. Those excellent gifts which were conferred on the apostate angels in their first creation were duly ordained by God to produce firm and constant obedience in them and to procure their beatitude; yet God knew they would be rebels and would never employ these gifts for the attainment of that good to which they were destined. The same can be said of Adam while still intact, whom God furnished with knowledge and holiness and fortified with his warnings abundantly sufficient to keep him in his duty; knowing meanwhile that all these things, which were applicable to promoting his obedience and happiness, would never be applied. It is therefore not alien to Divine wisdom to establish and ordain means applicable to some end, although he understands that, some obstacle intervening which he himself has not decreed to remove, the application itself will be hindered. Here that of Aquinas can be brought, in the disputed questions on Predestination, where he sets a difference between providence commonly taken and predestination, which is a special part of providence: Providence, he says, regards only the order unto the end; predestination regards the issue or event of the order. Things ordained to an end by that more common providence do not always attain the end; but those ordained by singular predestination always attain it. As therefore God, by that wider providence, is understood to have provided many bodily remedies applicable to driving away any bodily diseases whatever from any persons whatever, which nevertheless he has not decreed to be infallibly applied to these or those singular persons; so also we affirm that God, from that philanthropy and more common providence, provided and ordained the blood of his Son as a remedy applicable to expiating the sins of any human beings whatever, although by singular predestination he has not decreed to render it applied to all and each. But to what end is it ordained as applicable to all, which is not intended to be infallibly applied to all? I answer: that from this the Divine liberty, mercy, and justice may shine more clearly, while that remedy which by God's ordination is applicable to any unto salvation is nevertheless applied only to certain human beings, God specially having mercy on them, and is not applied to others, God permitting it, and their own malice deserving it.

source_text:
Obj. 3. Si mors Christi, Deo ordinante, sit remedium omnibus applicabile ad salutem, tum procuraret Deus hanc mortem Christi omnibus annunciandam, ne quis obtendere possit se tam efficacis remedii sola ignorantia periisse. At experientia docet hoc remedium non modo multis singularibus hominibus, sed etiam multis nationibus, per aliquot saecula non fuisse revelatum: Non ergo constitutum est a Deo remedium omnibus et singulis applicabile, quod tot homines latuit, Deo ipso ita rem disponente.

Sol. Ad minorem quod attinet, eam lubenter concedimus: quam et sacrae Scripturae testantur, et Patres agnoscunt esse verissimam. Act. xiv. 16. ostendit Paulus Deum praeteritis generationibus dimisisse omnes gentes ingredi vias suas, sine ulla Christi cognitione. Atque hanc ob causam Col. i. 26, 27. appellat Christi Evangelium mysterium quod absconditum fuit a saeculis et generationibus, nunc autem manifestatum est sanctis, quibus voluit Deus notas facere divitias, etc. Hinc illud Prosperi, De lib. arbitr.: Non remotum est ab inspectione communi, quot saeculis quam innumera hominum millia erroribus suis impietatibusque dimissa sine ulla veri Dei cognitione defecerint. Et De vocat. Gent. l. 2. c. 7.: In extremis mundi partibus sunt aliquae nationes, quibus nondum gratia Salvatoris illuxit. Concessa itaque Minore, dicimus consequentiam Majoris esse invalidam. Deus enim non tenetur procurare applicationem ejus remedii omnibus et singulis, quod omnibus et singulis voluit esse applicabile: quod tam in corporalibus quam spiritualibus remediis perspicuum est. Quamvis igitur mors Christi, ex ordinatione Dei et natura rei, sit ejusmodi remedium, quod possit omnibus et singulis humani generis individuis ad remissionem peccatorum et annunciari et applicari; tamen Deus nullo promisso tenetur procurare ut annuncietur et de facto applicetur omnibus et singulis. Voluit Deus Filii sui mortem esse thesaurum in manus suas quasi depositum, unde toti humano generi possit dispensare quicquid spectat sive ad veniam, sive ad gratiam, sive ad gloriam obtinendam; sed voluit etiam hujus thesauri communicationem actualem in liberrima sua potestate manere, atque inde donare vel non donare hominibus pro beneplacito voluntatis suae. Annon licet mihi quod volo facere de meo? Matth. xx. 15. Dicimus ergo mortem Christi ex Dei ordinatione esse omnibus applicabilem, non tamen Deum obligatum esse ad procurandam cuivis actualem ejus applicationem aut etiam annunciationem.
english: Obj. 3. If Christ's death, God so ordaining, is a remedy applicable to all unto salvation, then God would procure that this death of Christ be announced to all, lest anyone be able to plead that he perished by mere ignorance of so efficacious a remedy. But experience teaches that this remedy has not been revealed, not only to many singular human beings, but even to many nations, through several ages: it has therefore not been constituted by God as a remedy applicable to all and each, which has lain hidden from so many human beings, God himself so disposing the matter.

Sol. As to the minor, we gladly concede it — which both the sacred Scriptures testify and the Fathers acknowledge to be most true. ([[Acts 14:16 >> Bible:Acts 14:16]]) shows Paul that God in past generations suffered all nations to walk in their own ways, without any knowledge of Christ. And for this cause ([[Colossians 1:26–27 >> Bible:Colossians 1:26]]): he calls Christ's Gospel a mystery which was hidden from ages and generations, but now has been manifested to the saints, to whom God willed to make known the riches, etc. Hence that of Prosper, On Free Choice: It is not remote from common inspection through how many ages how innumerable thousands of human beings, dismissed to their errors and impieties, have perished without any knowledge of the true God. And On the Calling of the Gentiles, book 2, chapter 7: In the farthest parts of the world there are some nations to whom the grace of the Savior has not yet shone. The Minor therefore being conceded, we say the consequence of the Major is invalid. For God is not bound to procure the application of that remedy to all and each which he willed to be applicable to all and each — which is clear both in bodily and in spiritual remedies. Although therefore Christ's death, by God's ordination and by the nature of the thing, is such a remedy as can both be announced and be applied to all and each individual of the human race unto remission of sins, yet God is bound by no promise to procure that it be announced and in fact applied to all and each. God willed the death of his Son to be a treasure as it were deposited in his hands, from which he can dispense to the whole human race whatever looks to obtaining either pardon, or grace, or glory; but he also willed that the actual communication of this treasure remain in his freest power, and from it to give or not to give to human beings according to the good pleasure of his will. Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with my own? ([[Matthew 20:15 >> Bible:Matthew 20:15]]). We say therefore that Christ's death is by God's ordination applicable to all, yet that God is not obliged to procure for anyone its actual application or even its announcement.

source_text:
Obj. 4. Si mors Christi consideranda sit tanquam remedium vel lytron ex ordinatione cuivis homini applicabile, tum etiam resurrectio, intercessio, mediatio Christi ad omnes spectabunt eodem modo: At Christus non est excitatus pro omnibus, non intercedit pro omnibus, non est Mediator omnium: Ergo nec mors ejus ad omnes extendenda est. Haec nunquam esse divellenda probatur ex Rom. viii. 34. ubi conjunguntur omnia: Christus est qui mortuus est, imo qui resurrexit, qui etiam est ad dextram Patris, postulans pro nobis. Et Rom. iv. 25. Docet Apostolus, propter quorum offensas mortuus est Christus, propter eorundem justificationem excitatum fuisse: Non est autem excitatus pro omnibus: Ergo nec mortuus.

Sol. Si defensionis nostrae ratio rite perpendatur, facile constabit haec omnia causae nostrae nihil afferre detrimenti. Non enim tuemur mortem Christi esse ex ordinatione Dei ita applicatam omnibus et singulis hominibus, ut propter hoc propitiatorium sacrificium reponantur illico universi in statum gratiae et salutis: neque illud defendimus, ex speciali intentione Dei et praedestinationis decreto hanc mortem Christi esse infallibiliter omnibus et singulis applicandam; sed hanc mortem, Deo ita ordinante et in verbo suo revelante, esse illud lytron, quo expiari possunt peccata quorumcunque hominum, praestitis conditionibus in Evangelio requisitis. Atque hinc est quod praeco Evangelicus, quemcunque hominem convenerit sub quacunque coeli plaga, potest confidenter illi annunciare in morte Filii Dei salutem parabilem, si crediderit. Hoc nulli angelorum lapsorum promitti potest. Unde clarum est, hanc conditionalem promissionem salutis in morte Christi, quae annunciari potest cuivis homini, fundatam esse in aliqua ordinatione voluntatis Divinae, quae homines universim et sigillatim spectat, angelos non spectat. Dicant autem adversarii quae haec sit ordinatio, si non sit illa quam nos afferimus, de morte Christi humano generi sub conditionibus Evangelicis applicabili. Hisce ita constitutis propius accedimus ad dictae objectionis solutionem; et affirmamus, pari jure resurrectionem, intercessionem et mediationem Christi ad omnes et singulos pertinere quo mors ipsa sive oblatio in cruce peracta. Nam ut vere cuivis homini annunciare possumus peccata ejus morte Christi esse ex ordinatione Dei expiabilia, et fore expiata, si modo crediderit in Christum; ita et vere annunciare possumus eundem Christum resuscitatum esse ut illum credentem justificet, exaltatum ad dextram Dei ut sua mediatione et meritis illum credentem in gratia apud Deum conservet, et tandem ad gloriam perducat. Non itaque ea divellimus quae Deus conjunxit, sed mortem, resurrectionem et intercessionem Christi nexu indissolubili conjunctas docemus, at diversimode. Si spectemus humanum genus universum, hoc est, omnes et singulos homines, tum dicimus, non modo mortem sed resurrectionem et intercessionem Christi ad illos spectare quoad possibilitatem fruendi hisce beneficiis, praesupposita fidei conditione: Si spectemus electos, affirmamus haec omnia ad eos spectare quoad infallibilitatem fruendi, ex destinata scilicet et in tempore illis donanda hac fidei conditione. Quamvis ergo speciali quadam ratione mors et resurrectio Christi, cum ingenti thesauro meritorum ejus, ad solos electos restringatur, (de quo postea disseremus) tamen non est negandum mortem ac merita Christi, qui sanus omnium naturam et unam omnium causam suscepit, esse ejusmodi quae possunt omnibus et singulis humanam naturam participantibus annunciari, offerri et per fidem applicari. Hoc ipse Christus satis clare indicavit, Johann. iii. 17, 18. hisce verbis, Non misit Deus Filium suum in mundum ut condemnet mundum, sed ut servetur mundus per eum. Qui credit in eum non condemnabitur: qui non credit jam condemnatus est, quia non credidit in nomen unigeniti Filii Dei. Illi igitur qui nunquam credunt aut credituri sunt, habuerunt tamen vitam in morte meritisque Christi ex ordinatione Dei parabilem, si credidissent.
english: Obj. 4. If Christ's death is to be considered as a remedy or lytron applicable to any human being by God's ordination, then Christ's resurrection, intercession, and mediation will likewise look to all in the same way. But Christ was not raised for all, does not intercede for all, is not the Mediator of all: therefore neither is his death to be extended to all. That these must never be torn apart is proved from ([[Romans 8:34 >> Bible:Romans 8:34]]), where all are joined together: It is Christ who died, yes rather who rose again, who is also at the right hand of the Father, making intercession for us. And ([[Romans 4:25 >> Bible:Romans 4:25]]): the Apostle teaches that for whose offenses Christ died, for their justification he was also raised: but he was not raised for all; therefore neither did he die for all.

Sol. If the reason of our defense is rightly weighed, it will easily appear that all this brings no detriment to our cause. For we do not maintain that Christ's death is, by God's ordination, so applied to all and each human being that on account of this propitiatory sacrifice the whole are immediately set back into a state of grace and salvation; nor do we defend that, from God's special intention and the decree of predestination, this death of Christ is to be applied infallibly to all and each; but that this death, God so ordaining and revealing it in his word, is that lytron by which the sins of any human beings whatsoever can be expiated, the conditions required in the Gospel being fulfilled. And hence it is that the Gospel preacher, whomever he meets under whatever sky, can confidently announce to him salvation obtainable in the death of the Son of God, if he believes. This can be promised to none of the fallen angels. Whence it is clear that this conditional promise of salvation in Christ's death, which can be announced to any human being, is founded in some ordination of the Divine will which regards human beings universally and individually, and does not regard angels. Let the adversaries say what this ordination is, if it is not that which we affirm — of Christ's death as applicable to the human race under the Gospel conditions. These things being so established, we come nearer to the solution of the said objection; and we affirm that Christ's resurrection, intercession, and mediation pertain to all and each by the same right as the death itself, or the oblation accomplished on the cross. For as we can truly announce to any human being that his sins are, by God's ordination, expiable by Christ's death, and will be expiated if only he believes in Christ; so also we can truly announce that the same Christ has been raised that he may justify that believer, exalted to the right hand of God that by his mediation and merits he may preserve that believer in grace with God, and at length lead him to glory. We do not therefore tear apart what God has joined, but teach that Christ's death, resurrection, and intercession are joined by an indissoluble bond — yet in different ways. If we look to the universal human race, that is, to all and each human being, then we say that not only the death but also the resurrection and intercession of Christ look to them as to the possibility of enjoying these benefits, the condition of faith being presupposed: if we look to the elect, we affirm that all these look to them as to the infallibility of enjoying them, from this condition of faith destined for them and to be given them in time. Although therefore in a certain special respect Christ's death and resurrection, with the vast treasure of his merits, are restricted to the elect alone (of which we shall treat later), yet it is not to be denied that the death and merits of Christ, who soundly assumed the nature of all and one cause of all, are of such a kind as can be announced, offered, and applied by faith to all and each who share human nature. Christ himself indicated this clearly enough in ([[John 3:17–18 >> Bible:John 3:17]]) in these words: God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world, but that the world through him might be saved. He that believes on him is not condemned: he that believes not is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God. Those therefore who never believe or will believe nonetheless had life obtainable in the death and merits of Christ by God's ordination, if they had believed.
